REFUTED. The finding misstates the invariant it cites, gets a step of its own causal chain wrong, and the regime where the cost would matter is already guarded.

1. The quoted invariant is not what the spec says. `review/recurring-exclusions-spec.md` §5.7 ("Perf invariant (the D7 of this issue)") reads in full: "`Exclusions == null` short-circuits before anything else in every new check. The A/B gate: the P-K cells (A4W, LRA in-memory, LRA SQLite, A4S SQLite) must show no measurable regression for schedules **without** exclusions, and the golden-JSON suite must show byte-identical serialization." D7 is scoped, by the authoritative spec, to the null-exclusion path — which the finding itself confirms is clean (RecurringTask.cs:639-640). The finding's complaint that "the spec's A/B gate does not measure it because it only compares schedules WITHOUT exclusions" is therefore describing the spec's deliberate scope, not an escape from it. §5.6 goes further and *accepts* the cost on the feature's own path in writing: "`CountMissedOccurrences` with exclusions always WALKS (the filtered door), honouring the caller's cap as today ... No closed-form region subtraction in v1 (complexity not bought by any decision path)."

2. The guard for the only regime with large step counts already exists and the spec names it. §5.6: "Skip-forward keeps its O(1)-ish contract on fine grids through §5.2's uniform-base jump ... a per-second grid after a month of downtime never walks millions of steps." That is RecurringTask.cs:946-960 — with `Exclusions != null` and a uniform base, it jumps on `Base()` (one clone per call) and filter-fixes; the walk is never entered. So gotcha 7 is preserved exactly where it matters.

3. The 2,000,000 figure is a termination bound, not a workload, and the code says so at RecurringTask.cs:904-906: "Next-run walk: only ever runs for non-uniform (calendar) schedules, which are coarse by nature (at most a few dozen occurrences/day), so this cap is never reached by a real schedule — it only guarantees termination against a pathological/misbehaving interval." The finding's own scenario, `EveryDay().AtTimes(09:00, 17:00)`, is 2 slots/day: a full year of downtime is ~730 walk steps, i.e. ~730 short-lived clones. Framing that as "once per step of the 2,000,000-iteration walk" inflates a bound into a cost.

4. Factual error in the causal chain. The finding claims "`FilterExcludedCandidates` re-enters `GetNextOccurrence` on the base copy at line 742 for the non-uniform branch", counted as "one [clone] per discarded candidate inside each `FilterExcludedCandidates` call". That re-entry is on `baseGrid`, whose `Exclusions` was set to null by `Base()` (line 1145), so it lands on the `Exclusions == null` fast path at 639-640 and allocates nothing. There is exactly ONE clone per outer `GetNextOccurrence` call regardless of how many candidates are discarded — the per-discard clones the scenario counts do not exist.

5. The premise "converts a pure-arithmetic walk into one object allocation per step" is false for the very scenario chosen. With exclusions present, each step necessarily runs `TryGetExclusionRegionExit` (764-794): a `WallClock.ToWall` timezone conversion, a `DateOnly` construction, and a LINEAR `Dates.Contains` over `DateOnly[]` (ScheduleExclusions.cs:16) — up to 300 comparisons for the finding's own 300-date holiday calendar — plus a range loop; and the zoned base grid itself runs `NextGridOccurrenceInZone` wall mapping. A single `MemberwiseClone` (one flat ~200-byte memcpy over ~20 fields, no field walking) is noise beside the work the feature does by construction. It is not the marginal cost, and removing it would not change the step's cost profile measurably.

6. The `CountMissedOccurrences` sub-claim is the weakest: reaching `MaxSkipCountIterations = 10_000` requires the calendar grid to actually own 10,000 occurrences in the span (13+ years of downtime at 2/day), and each of those steps already executes the full grid cascade. 10k transient sub-200-byte objects is a fraction of one Gen0 budget, collected in a single gen0 pass, on a once-per-recovery diagnostic path.

Residual truth: `Base()` is trivially hoistable (cache it on the instance, or thread the base grid through the walk) and doing so would be a harmless micro-optimization. But no invariant is violated, no guard is missing, the correctness is conceded by the finding itself, and the allocation is dominated by the exclusion check it accompanies. P2 is not defensible; this is at most a nit.

REFUTED — the per-probe scan is bounded by an explicit design guard, and the cited cost chain does not multiply out.

1) The size cap already IS the per-probe bound, by design. `ValidateExclusions` (RecurringTask.cs:285-289) refuses `Dates.Length + Ranges.Length > 1000` — a COMBINED cap, not 1000 each. The finding's "~1000 date comparisons plus ~1000 range comparisons" (~2000/probe, 4x10^8 total) is impossible; the ceiling is 1000 comparisons/probe. And spec §3.2 states this explicitly: "**Size cap**: `Dates.Length + Ranges.Length <= 1000` after normalization... The cap bounds the definition's size **and the per-probe exclusion work**". So the spec's "predictable cost per probe" is delivered by the cap; §3.2's sort/merge is claimed for "one canonical serialized form", never for O(log n) lookup. The invariant the finding cites is not the one the spec states.

2) The headline scenario cannot reach the budget at all. `Every(1).Minutes()` + `OnDates(900)` + 100 ranges: `Base()` (RecurringTask.cs:1142-1148, exclusions cleared) satisfies `IsUniformGrid()` (:1248-1277 — pure minute cadence, no zone, no cron), so `AdvanceBasePastExcludedRegion` (:716-733) takes the `TryJumpBaseUniformGrid` branch and each discard jumps to the first base slot on/after the region EXIT in O(1). Candidates advance monotonically and a finite date/range region is exited exactly once, so discards are bounded by regions crossed — at most ~1000, not 200,000. Worst case for that schedule is ~1000 probes x 1000 comparisons = ~10^6 comparisons, sub-millisecond. That is precisely spec §5.2's contract ("an every-minute cron crossing a 30-day window must cost ~1 probe, not 43,200").

3) The only definitions that can actually spend 200k discards are the repeating-`Days` ones (the spec's own `Every(7).Days()` on a Saturday anchor + `Except(Saturday)`), and there the scan is short-circuited: :774 is `Days.Contains(dow) || Dates.Contains(localDate)` — when the weekday matches, `Dates.Contains` never runs. Those definitions are also gated: spec §5.4 / §"Emptiness & budget" makes the empty-forever cadence "refused at dispatch by the budget", i.e. the cost is paid once on the dispatching caller and ends in a typed refusal; it never reaches a worker, and a later empty-forever definition can only arrive through Reschedule, which validates and refuses a definition with no occurrence left before writing. The "worker blocked holding `_inFlightTasks` and the registry entry" scenario therefore has no reachable trigger.

4) The interruptibility invariant is misquoted. `src/EverTask/CLAUDE.md`'s "every entry point hands it the CALLER's token" is about "a grid that may do real I/O" — the async `INextOccurrenceProvider` path; the built-in arithmetic has always been synchronous and uncancellable, bounded by iteration caps that predate #36 (`MaxWallMappingIterations` 100_000 at :627, `MaxNextRunWalkIterations` 2_000_000 at :907, `MaxSkipCountIterations` 10_000). #36 adds no new class of uncancellable loop; it adds one more cap.

5) The "2M x fresh 200k budget" multiplication is not real: a door call that spends its budget THROWS (:707-708), so the walk cannot chain full budgets; and `NextOccurrenceStrictlyAfter` reaches the walk only for non-uniform calendar grids (:939-960 jumps first for uniform and for an exclusions-carrying uniform base), whose density the spec bounds at "a handful of slots per day". The `Base()` MemberwiseClone is one shallow clone per door call, the existing `Unbounded()` precedent.

What survives is a micro-optimization, not a defect: with merged, non-overlapping ranges at most one can cover a candidate, so the `Ranges` loop (:784-791) could `break` on the first hit and both lookups could binary-search the sorted arrays. Worth doing, but the worst case it removes is ~10^6 comparisons on any schedule that passes ingress; P2 impact (blocked worker, unstoppable shutdown, ~4x10^8 comparisons) is not supported.

D7 is explicitly scoped to exclusion-free schedules; the finding restates it as the broader "must not regress the grid's cost profile", then itself concedes the Exclusions==null fast path (RecurringTask.cs:639-640) is clean. Its complaint that the A/B gate "only compares schedules WITHOUT exclusions" is the spec's deliberate scope, not a gap.

(2) The 2,000,000-step walk is unreachable for the scenario named, and the spec explains why. MaxNextRunWalkIterations (line 907) is a termination guard, not an achievable step count. Spec §5.6: "Skip-forward keeps its O(1)-ish contract on fine grids through §5.2's uniform-base jump... a per-second grid after a month of downtime never walks millions of steps" — that is the jump branch at 946-960, which allocates ONE Base() per call, not one per step. The walk at 962-976 handles only coarse calendar schedules. The finding's own scenario, EveryDay().AtTimes(09:00,17:00), steps twice per day: a one-year outage is ~730 clones (~150 KB), a decade ~7,300; 2M steps would need ~2,700 years of downtime. The repro cannot be built at the claimed scale — it pairs the guard constant with a grid shape that can never approach it, while the shapes that could are routed to the jump.

(3) A factual error in the causal chain. The scenario claims "one per discarded candidate inside each FilterExcludedCandidates call". False: FilterExcludedCandidates (686-714) reuses the single baseGrid for every discarded candidate. AdvanceBasePastExcludedRegion goes to TryJumpBaseUniformGrid, or baseGrid.CronInterval.GetNextOccurrence, or GetNextBaseOccurrence -> baseGrid.GetNextOccurrence where baseGrid.Exclusions == null, hitting the 639-640 fast path. Zero clones inside the discard loop; exactly one clone per GetNextOccurrence call regardless of region count.

(4) The allocation is dominated by per-step work already present, so it is not a "pure-arithmetic walk" converted into an allocating one. A ~200-byte pointer-bump gen0 allocation that dies immediately is a small fraction of that; the O(|Dates|) linear scan would be the real per-step cost, and the finding does not raise it.

ledger.title: The exclusion-budget schedule retry re-executes the run it just recorded (storage-backed path)
ledger.invariant: A recurring run that has been RECORDED against the row (CurrentRunCount incremented, Completed/UpdateCurrentRun written) is never delivered a second time by EverTask's own schedule-retry or recovery paths. The cursor a schedule row carries names a PENDING slot; the recovery grace window (`Dispatcher.IsSlipedOccurrenceStillCurrentAsync`) exists precisely to run a slot that has NOT run yet. src/EverTask/CLAUDE.md states the sibling rule for the provider path — "the write and the next cursor are one operation, so the row is left as a crash between a side effect and its write leaves it, and at-least-once covers the replay" — i.e. the provider retry may replay only because NOTHING was written.
ledger.causal_chain: Spec §5.4 deliberately inverts the provider contract for the exclusion budget: the run is recorded FIRST and the cursor is RETAINED. `RecordRunBeforeExclusionRetryAsync` (WorkerExecutor.cs:1774-1808) writes `CompleteRecurringRun/UpdateCurrentRun(id, ms, retainedCursor = rowCursor ?? scheduledTime, ...)`, so the row ends up with `CurrentRunCount = N+1` AND `NextRunUtc = S`, the slot that just executed. `DeferScheduleForExclusionAsync` (1810-1832) then parks a schedule-retry delivery carrying `ScheduleRunAlreadyRecorded = true` and `ScheduleRetryFromUtc = S`. When that retry fires, `RetryScheduleDecisionAsync` splits: the storage-LESS branch (WorkerExecutor.cs:441-454) correctly resumes the interrupted ADVANCE — `QueueNextOccourrence(resumed, ..., countsAsRun: !task.ScheduleRunAlreadyRecorded)` → false, so nothing is re-run and nothing is double-counted. The storage-BACKED branch (WorkerExecutor.cs:485-487) instead throws the marker away and re-dispatches the ROW: `dispatcher.ExecuteDispatch(recovered.Task, row.NextRunUtc /* = S */, definition, row.CurrentRunCount, ..., isRecovery: true, ...)`. Inside `DecideRecurringRunAsync` (Dispatcher.cs:1016-1075) S is normalized (it is a legal grid slot, so it comes back unchanged), it is not `> nowUtc`, and the grace-window branch `isRecovery && IsSlipedOccurrenceStillCurrentAsync(recurring, S, nowUtc, ...)` answers TRUE whenever S's natural successor is still in the future — the normal state seconds after a run on any cadence coarser than the retry backoff. The dispatcher therefore returns `RecurringRunDecision(S, false)`, logs `RecoveryExecutingSlippedOccurrence`, and parks the schedule at S, which is in the past, so the scheduler fires it immediately and the handler runs again. The same hole reopens on restart: the row on disk carries no marker distinguishing "this cursor's run already happened" from "this cursor is pending" (`ScheduleRunAlreadyRecorded` is memory-only, TaskHandlerExecutor.cs:97-101), so startup recovery re-dispatches S through the identical grace window.

Verdict: the fix (fall back to the walk on a null jump, as :941-944 does) is correct and worth making, but this is hardening against a definition the supported API cannot construct, not the P1 data-loss path the finding claims. Confidence medium: the mechanism is proven by numeric construction; the severity/reachability claim does not hold.

The finding's causal chain is real as written, but its *trigger* does not exist: for any definition that passes `IsUniformGrid()`, the self-verify at `RecurringTask.cs:1331` provably cannot fail, so `TryJumpBaseUniformGrid` never returns the "fall back to the walk" null at :722. The guard is `IsUniformGrid()` itself, together with the shape of `RunIntervalCascade`.

**1. The claimed "non-constant uniform grid" is not constructible.**
`IsUniformGrid()` (`:1248-1277`) requires: `Exclusions == null` (true on the `Base()` copy), `GoverningZone == null`, no provider, no cron, no `MonthInterval`, `HourInterval.OnHours` empty, `DayInterval`/`WeekInterval` `OnDays` empty and `OnTimes.Length <= 1`. With those constraints, `GetNextOccurrence` is `NextGridOccurrenceUtc -> RunIntervalCascade` (`:890-900`), and every surviving stage is either a fixed translation or a translation followed by a snap to an *absolute, phase-independent* value:
- `SecondInterval` (`SecondInterval.cs:24`): `current.AddSeconds(I)` — pure translation.
- `MinuteInterval` (`MinuteInterval.cs:31-32`): `+I minutes`, then `Adjust(second: OnSecond)` — snap to a constant.
- `HourInterval` (`HourInterval.cs:52-62`): `+I hours`, then `Adjust(minute/second)` to constants; `NextValidHour` is unreachable because `OnHours` must be empty.
- `DayInterval` (`DayInterval.cs:63-68`) and `WeekInterval` (`WeekInterval.cs:61-66`): the `OnDays` branch (`NextDayOfWeekSlot`, the only phase-dependent one) is unreachable — `OnDays` must be empty; the remaining branch is `AddDays(k)` then `GetNextRequestedTime`. With `OnTimes.Length <= 1` and `Interval > 0` (their own `Validate()` throws for `Interval == 0 && OnDays.Length == 0`), `nextDay.Date != current.Date` is *always* true, so both arms of `GetNextRequestedTime` (`DateTimeExtensions.cs:36-49`) select index 0 and the result is `Date(current) + k days @ T`, independent of the input's time-of-day.

So the composed map is either `t -> t + c` (sub-day cadences only) or `t -> Date(t) + K days + fixed time-of-day` (a Day/Week interval present). In both cases consecutive occurrences differ by a constant, so `previous = candidate - stepTicks` is a genuine grid point and `GetNextOccurrence(previous) == candidate` holds. The XML doc's "a non-constant combination safely falls back to the walk" is defensive belt-and-braces, not a reachable case — which is why `RecurringSkipForwardHardeningTests.cs:18-41` only exercises combos that *are* constant (`Minute(5)+Second(30)`, `Hour(2)+Minute(15)`) and pins the calendar cases as `IsUniformGrid() == false`.

**2. The finding's own worked example is arithmetically constant.** `DayInterval{Interval=2}` (default `OnTimes = [00:00]`) + `HourInterval{Interval=7}`: cascade gives `Date(t)+2d @ 00:00`, then `+7h` = `Date(t)+2d @ 07:00`. From `Jan 1 07:00` the series is `Jan 3 07:00, Jan 5 07:00, ...` — a constant 2-day step. The self-verify passes; step 4 of the scenario never happens.

**3. The `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` variant is intended behaviour, not an inconsistency.** On the base grid `GoverningZone` is null (guaranteed by `IsUniformGrid`), so no `TimeZoneInfo` conversion runs inside the jump; the only AOORE source is `DateTimeOffset` overflow near `MaxValue`. Mapping that to "no occurrence" is the *documented* decision for the whole exclusion path — `GetNextBaseOccurrence` (`:738-748`) does exactly the same with an explicit rationale ("An exclusion search may legitimately reach the end of DateTimeOffset"), and the spec §5.2 calls end-of-representable-time "the genuine end of representable time". The same applies to `jumps >= maxJumps` (`:1311-1313`), which is only reachable when the region exit sits at the top of the representable range.

**4. The cited invariant is honoured where it actually applies.** Spec §2.6 / gotcha 20's "computational exhaustion is never mathematical exhaustion" is about the 200,000-candidate search budget, and `FilterExcludedCandidates:707-708` throws `ExclusionSearchBudgetExceededException` rather than returning null — exactly as required. The remaining null reasons in `TryJumpUniformGrid` (`first == null`, `second == null`, `stepTicks <= 0` — itself unreachable since `NextGridOccurrenceUtc` enforces `>= current + 1s`) are all genuine mathematical ends the non-exclusion path would answer identically.

The asymmetry with `NextOccurrenceStrictlyAfter:946-960` (which *does* fall through to the walk on a null) is real but is defence-in-depth on a path that also has a cheap walk available; it does not evidence a reachable defect at :722. Residual: if a future interval type with phase-dependent spacing were added and admitted by `IsUniformGrid`, :722 would need the same fall-through — worth a comment at most, not a P1.

ledger.title: TryGetExclusionRegionExit dereferences the exclusion arrays without the null tolerance its three siblings implement
ledger.invariant: A hand-built or hand-edited definition fails as typed, validated metadata (ArgumentException → poison path), never with a NullReferenceException out of the occurrence math. The exclusions feature adopts this rule explicitly everywhere else: `ValidateExclusions` repairs nulls (RecurringTask.cs:233-235), `HasCalendarExclusions()` is written `(exclusions.Days?.Length ?? 0) > 0` (RecurringTask.cs:400-402) because spec §4.2 requires it to run BEFORE `Validate()`, and `AppendExclusions` uses `exclusions.Days ?? []` (RecurringTask.cs:1443-1445).
ledger.causal_chain: `ScheduleExclusions.Days/Dates/Ranges` are plain `{ get; set; }` array properties with collection initializers and no converter (ScheduleExclusions.cs:13-20), so System.Text.Json writes a literal JSON `null` straight through the setter — which is exactly why `ValidateExclusions` opens with `exclusions.Days ??= []`. `TryGetExclusionRegionExit` is the per-candidate predicate on the evaluation path and reads `exclusions.Days.Length`, `exclusions.Dates.Length`, `exclusions.Days.Contains(...)`, `exclusions.Dates.Contains(...)` and `foreach (var range in exclusions.Ranges)` unguarded (RecurringTask.cs:769-791). `CalculateNextRun` / `CalculateNextValidRun` are PUBLIC surface (RecurringTask.cs:410-419, RecurringTaskExtensions.cs:42-49) and do not call `Validate()` themselves — only the library's own ingress and recovery paths do — so any consumer reaching the grid without validating gets an NRE from inside the scheduler instead of the documented ArgumentException.
ledger.failure_scenario: `var t = new RecurringTask { HourInterval = new HourInterval(1), Exclusions = new ScheduleExclusions { Days = null! } }; t.CalculateNextRun(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow, 1);` → NullReferenceException at RecurringTask.cs:769. The same shape arrives from a row whose JSON was hand-edited to `"Exclusions":{"Days":null,"Dates":["2026-12-25"],"Ranges":[]}` and is then evaluated by a component that reached the definition without the validate gate; the corrupt-metadata contract promises `ArgumentException`/poison, not an NRE.
ledger.evidence: RecurringTask.cs:769 `if (exclusions.Days.Length > 0 || exclusions.Dates.Length > 0)` and RecurringTask.cs:784 `foreach (var range in exclusions.Ranges)`, against the deliberate null-tolerance at RecurringTask.cs:233-235 (`exclusions.Days ??= []`), RecurringTask.cs:400-402 (`(exclusions.Days?.Length ?? 0) > 0`) and RecurringTask.cs:1443-1445 (`var days = exclusions.Days ?? [];`). Public entry points: RecurringTask.cs:410 `public DateTimeOffset? CalculateNextRun(...)`, RecurringTaskExtensions.cs:42 `public static NextRunResult CalculateNextValidRun(...)`.
ledger.fix_sketch: Either make the three properties null-rejecting at the setter (`set => _days = value ?? [];`, matching `DayInterval.OnTimes`'s null-tolerant setter), or apply the same `?? []` guard inside `TryGetExclusionRegionExit`. The setter fix is the stronger one: it removes the class of bug for every future reader of the arrays.

votes.reasoning:
REFUTED. Three independent guards already stand between the described corruption and RecurringTask.cs:769, and the finding's own authority (the spec) places null-leniency exactly where the code places it.

1) The persisted-JSON half of the scenario has no component to land in. `EverTaskJson.Deserialize<RecurringTask>` appears in exactly two places in src/: `src/EverTask/Worker/RecoveredTaskFactory.cs:87`, which calls `recurring?.Validate(providers)` on the very next line (:93) inside the same try, with the explicit comment that a schedule which deserializes but is corrupt must be validated HERE so the caller's poison guard sees it; and `src/Monitoring/EverTask.Monitor.Api/Services/TaskScheduleFacts.cs:121`, which only reads `OccurrenceMode`/`Misfire?.Policy`/`TimeZoneId` off the object and never asks the grid anything. There is no third deserializer, so "a component that reached the definition without the validate gate" does not exist in this repo. The other two ingress points validate first too: `Dispatcher.ExecuteDispatchCore` runs `recurring?.Validate(Providers)` as its first statement (Dispatcher.cs:393), before the clock is even read, and `TaskScheduleManager` at :367. And note `ValidateExclusions` REPAIRS nulls (`??= []`, RecurringTask.cs:233-235) — it does not throw — so the hand-edited `"Days":null` row does not even reach the poison path: it is normalized and runs correctly. The finding's "corrupt-metadata contract promises ArgumentException, not an NRE" mischaracterizes the contract: the spec's own table (review/recurring-exclusions-spec.md:372) reads "`null` arrays on a hand-built `ScheduleExclusions` | `Validate()` | read as empty", while :378 reserves `ArgumentException` for a null Ranges ELEMENT / bad DayOfWeek / inverted range. Null arrays are explicitly a Validate()-repairs case, assigned to Validate() and to nothing else.

2) The "three siblings" are not evidence of a codebase-wide null-tolerance policy at evaluation time; each is null-tolerant for a documented reason that does not apply here, and all three run OUTSIDE the post-validation math. `ValidateExclusions` IS the repair. `HasCalendarExclusions()` (RecurringTask.cs:400-402) is called from `ScheduleTimeZone.ApplyDefault` (ScheduleTimeZone.cs:120), the ingress default-zone stamp, and spec:163 states the reason verbatim — "`ApplyDefault` must tolerate `null` arrays (it can run before `Validate()` canonicalizes...)". `AppendExclusions` (:1440) builds the human-readable description, a diagnostic that may be called on any object at any time. `TryGetExclusionRegionExit` is in the opposite class: it is unreachable except from inside `GetNextOccurrence`/`FilterExcludedCandidates` (:698, :957), i.e. strictly downstream of the validation gate, and it opens with `var exclusions = Exclusions!;` — the `!` is the author stating that contract.

3) The only scenario that survives is a caller-contract violation the compiler itself refuses. `ScheduleExclusions.Days/Dates/Ranges` are declared non-nullable with `= []` initializers (ScheduleExclusions.cs:13-20); the finding's repro must literally write `Days = null!` — an explicit null-forgiving suppression of CS8625 — then skip every library ingress and call the low-level public math directly. The consequence is a synchronous NullReferenceException handed straight back to the statement that built the object: no persisted corruption, no scheduler stall, no bypass of the poison path, nothing a recovery predicate can be left holding.

Residual: the dereference is technically reachable through public surface (`CalculateNextRun`, `CalculateNextValidRun` are public and do not self-validate), and a consumer project compiled with nullable disabled would take `Days = null` without a warning. Adding `?? []` would cost nothing. But that is a P4 defensive nicety on a deliberately-annotated contract, not a P2 defect: no library path can produce the state, and the spec assigns null-array leniency to `Validate()`, which is where the code implements it.

The unguarded deref is real (RecurringTask.cs:769/784 reached via 639 -> 686 -> 698), and a direct `new ScheduleExclusions { Days = null! }` + public `CalculateNextRun` does NRE. But it is not a defect against the authoritative contract:

(1) No reachable path. Every site that accepts a hand-built or deserialized definition validates before asking the grid: Dispatcher.cs:393, TaskScheduleManager.cs:367, RecoveredTaskFactory.cs:93 (the only Deserialize<RecurringTask> feeding execution). ValidateExclusions (233-235) repairs Days/Dates/Ranges in place. The only other deserializer, Monitor.Api Services/TaskScheduleFacts.cs:121, reads OccurrenceMode/Misfire/TimeZoneId only and never evaluates the grid. The finding's hand-edited-JSON scenario needs "a component that reached the definition without the validate gate" and names none; none exists.

(2) The spec places the repair exactly where the code puts it. review/recurring-exclusions-spec.md:372 "null arrays on a hand-built ScheduleExclusions | Validate() | read as empty", and :163 gives the sole tolerance carve-out: "ApplyDefault must tolerate null arrays (it can run before Validate())" — that is HasCalendarExclusions (400-402). The other cited sibling, AppendExclusions (1440-1448), is ToString(), which must never throw. So the two null-tolerant siblings are documented pre-Validate/never-throw surfaces, not evidence of a universal rule the evaluation predicate broke.

(3) The claimed invariant ("corrupt metadata -> ArgumentException, never NRE from the occurrence math") is not a property this class has for unvalidated input, and the exclusions feature is strictly better than the precedent: HourInterval.Validate() does `foreach (var hour in OnHours)` and DayInterval.Validate() does `OnDays.Length` — both NRE (inside Validate itself) on a hand-edited "OnHours":null / "OnDays":null; ToString derefs OnHours/OnTimes/OnDays/OnMonths unguarded at 1391-1430. Only DayInterval.OnTimes was hardened, and its comment says why: that null crashed the deserialize itself, a genuinely pre-Validate failure. Exclusions, unlike those, are actually repaired by Validate.

(4) What is left is caller misuse: Days is a non-nullable DayOfWeek[] with a collection initializer, so the repro requires `null!` (or reflection) to defeat the annotation and then bypass the validation gate.

A defensive `??= []` would be harmless, but as a P2 with a concrete failing sequence the finding does not stand.

ledger.title: Cron region-jump test cannot distinguish the O(1) jump from a 43,200-step walk
ledger.invariant: Spec §5.2: "Cron never walks an excluded region slot by slot — an every-minute cron crossing a 30-day window must cost ~1 probe, not 43,200." The named claim is a COST claim, and the cost is what the code path in `AdvanceBasePastExcludedRegion` exists for.
ledger.causal_chain: `Should_jump_a_minute_cron_across_a_thirty_day_window` asserts only `task.CalculateNextRun(start.AddMinutes(-1), 1).ShouldBe(exit)`. If the cron branch (RecurringTask.cs:724-730) were removed, control would fall to `GetNextBaseOccurrence(baseGrid, candidate, ...)` — one anchored Cronos step per excluded minute. 30 days of minutes is 43,200 discarded candidates, comfortably under `MaxExclusionSearchIterations = 200_000`, so the loop still terminates and still returns exactly `exit`. The assertion is identical under both implementations.
ledger.failure_scenario: Someone refactors `AdvanceBasePastExcludedRegion` and drops or mis-orders the cron branch (it currently sits after the `IsUniformGrid()` check and is reached only because cron forces `IsUniformGrid()` false). The suite stays green while an every-minute cron with a maintenance window now spends 43,200 Cronos calls on every single door call — and `CountMissedOccurrences`, which calls the door up to 10,000 times, becomes hundreds of millions of probes.
ledger.evidence: test/EverTask.Tests/RecurringTests/RecurringExclusionMathTests.cs:154-169 (result-only assertion); src/EverTask/Scheduler/Recurring/RecurringTask.cs:719-730 (`IsUniformGrid()` guard first, then the cron branch); RecurringTask.cs:629 (`MaxExclusionSearchIterations = 200_000` > 43,200).
ledger.fix_sketch: Count the probes: wrap the cron oracle (or assert on iteration count via a widened budget) so the test fails when the crossing costs more than a small constant — e.g. temporarily assert against a definition whose region is wide enough that a per-slot walk would exceed the budget and throw, or expose a counter the test can read. The `fineGrid` half of `Should_skip_forward_on_the_uniform_base_and_match_a_walked_reference` already uses the first technique correctly (a per-second grid over 30 days exceeds `MaxNextRunWalkIterations`), so the pattern exists in the same file.

ledger.title: ET0010's forward chain walk can never traverse a conversion node
ledger.invariant: Spec §4.2: "The analyzer must consider the completed chain: any `Except`/`ExceptWeekends` call anywhere in it suppresses the diagnostic (conservative, keeps the zero-false-positive bar)." The forward half of `HasExclusionInCompletedChain` is what covers calls that come AFTER `InTimeZone`.
ledger.causal_chain: `TryGetOuterInvocation` walks up through implicit conversions with `while (current.Parent is IConversionOperation conversion) current = conversion;`, so on exit `current` IS the conversion node. It then tests `ReferenceEquals(Unwrap(outer.Instance), current)` — but `Unwrap` strips conversions, returning the INNER invocation, never the conversion node. So whenever a conversion sits between two chain steps the comparison is `ReferenceEquals(innerInvocation, conversionNode)`, which is always false, `TryGetOuterInvocation` returns false, and the forward walk stops at the first conversion instead of continuing to the `ExceptWeekends()` beyond it. The backward walk (line 145-152) gets this right because it calls `Unwrap(step)` on both sides consistently.
ledger.failure_scenario: Any future chain step whose receiver needs an implicit reference conversion — for instance adding a base-interface member that is NOT redeclared with `new` on the derived builder, or a new builder interface that inherits `IBuildableSchedulerBuilder` without redeclaring `Except`/`ExceptWeekends` — puts a conversion node between `InTimeZone(...)` and the later `ExceptWeekends()`. ET0010 then fires on `Schedule().EveryHour().InTimeZone("Europe/Rome").<something>().ExceptWeekends()`, a chain `Validate()` accepts: a false positive on a warning that is a build error under the repo's analyzer ruleset. It is latent today only because every Elapsed-capable builder interface (`IHourSchedulerBuilder`, `IMinuteSchedulerBuilder`, `IIntervalSchedulerBuilder`) is standalone and `IBuildableSchedulerBuilder` returns itself, so no conversion is emitted — which is also why the four new `Et0010ScheduleTimeZoneTests` cases cannot detect it.
ledger.evidence: analyzers/EverTask.Analyzers/ScheduleTimeZoneAnalyzer.cs:166-180 (`TryGetOuterInvocation`: the walk-up loop at 171-172 vs the `ReferenceEquals(Unwrap(outer.Instance), current)` test at 177); contrast the consistent `Unwrap(step)` in the backward walk at lines 145-152. New tests at test/EverTask.Analyzers.Tests/Et0010ScheduleTimeZoneTests.cs:64-70 all use `EveryHour()` → `IHourSchedulerBuilder`, a standalone interface, so no conversion node is produced.
ledger.fix_sketch: Keep the pre-walk operand as the identity being matched: `IOperation current = operation; while (current.Parent is IConversionOperation c) current = c;` then compare with `ReferenceEquals(Unwrap(outer.Instance), Unwrap(current))`, or simply `ReferenceEquals(Unwrap(outer.Instance), operation)`.

votes.reasoning:
Attempted refutation via an existing-guard lens; the guard hypothesis (no conversion node is ever emitted, so the walk is a harmless no-op) held for the finding's stated scenario but failed overall, so the finding survives with corrections.

Empirical verification: I added a temporary probe test against the real ScheduleTimeZoneAnalyzer in test/EverTask.Analyzers.Tests (deleted afterwards; the untracked ZzTempConversionReproTests.cs belongs to another agent and was left untouched) and ran dotnet test.

(1) The finding's own scenario does NOT reproduce. With stubs where IHourSchedulerBuilder : IBuildableSchedulerBuilder inherits Except/ExceptWeekends WITHOUT `new` — precisely "a base-interface member not redeclared with new" — the chain r.Schedule().EveryHour().InTimeZone("Europe/Rome").ExceptWeekends() reported nothing, while the negative control r.Schedule().EveryHour().InTimeZone("Europe/Rome") on the same derived interface DID report ET0010. Roslyn emits no IConversionOperation for an implicit derived-interface to base-interface receiver conversion, so the forward walk traverses that step correctly. The finding's causal premise about how a conversion node arises, and its prediction that a future interface refactor of that shape would expose the bug, are both wrong.

(2) The ReferenceEquals defect itself is real and reachable TODAY. With an explicit cast producing a genuine conversion node — ((IBuildableSchedulerBuilder)r.Schedule().EveryHour().InTimeZone("Europe/Rome")).ExceptWeekends() — the analyzer emitted ET0010 (expected 0 diagnostics, got 1: warning ET0010 at (6,63)-(6,88)). That is a false positive on a chain that carries an exclusion, violating spec 4.2 ("any Except/ExceptWeekends call anywhere in it suppresses the diagnostic"), and ET0010 is a build error under the repo ruleset.

Code reading confirmed at analyzers/EverTask.Analyzers/ScheduleTimeZoneAnalyzer.cs:166-185: the walk-up loop (171-172) leaves `current` AS the conversion node, while Unwrap(outer.Instance) (177) strips conversions to the inner invocation, making the comparison unsatisfiable whenever a conversion separates chain steps; the backward walk (145-152) is correct because it Unwraps both sides. The code-level defect is confirmed by experiment, though the finding's stated scenario is disproven and its severity overstated.

CONFIRMED (mechanism): In TryGetOuterInvocation (ScheduleTimeZoneAnalyzer.cs:166-185), the walk-up loop at 171-172 leaves `current` pointing AT the outermost conversion node, while line 177 tests ReferenceEquals(Unwrap(outer.Instance), current) — Unwrap strips conversions and returns the inner invocation, so the comparison can never be true when a conversion is present. The forward half of HasExclusionInCompletedChain therefore stops dead at the first conversion. The backward walk (144-151) is consistent because it Unwraps both sides. Fix is one token: Unwrap(current).

REFUTED (stated scenario): I built the finding's exact scenario as a test in test/EverTask.Analyzers.Tests (the stubs are per-test source, so I declared IHourSchedulerBuilder : IBuildableSchedulerBuilder with ExceptWeekends inherited and NOT redeclared with `new`) and ran `r.Schedule().EveryHour().InTimeZone("Europe/Rome").ExceptWeekends()`. The analyzer stayed SILENT — no false positive. That is a genuine false positive on a warning that is a build error under the repo ruleset, and it is constructible against the real API today (interface-to-interface cast is legal C#; the concrete builder implements both). It is however contrived — nobody would cast, since ExceptWeekends is already on IHourSchedulerBuilder.

Verdict: not refuted, because a concrete failing sequence exists and the cited line-177 defect is exactly its cause; but the finding should be downgraded — the described scenario is empirically false, and the only reachable trigger requires a deliberate mid-chain cast. Temp probe file was deleted; tree is clean.

ledger.title: The exclusion filter loop has no forward-progress guard, unlike every other walk in the file
ledger.invariant: Gotcha 7: the skip-forward primitive "must never return a value <= after" and every walk in this file carries an explicit no-progress bail — `if (next.Value <= occurrence) return null;` (RecurringTask.cs:973), `if (next is null || next <= current) return null;` (RecurringTask.cs:1017). The anchored-advance loop introduced by #36 carries none.
ledger.causal_chain: `FilterExcludedCandidates` (686-714) assigns `candidate = AdvanceBasePastExcludedRegion(baseGrid, current, exit.Value, ...)` and loops on nothing but `candidate != null`. The cron branch (724-730) computes the next occurrence from `exit.AddTicks(-1)` — an ABSOLUTE instant that is never compared against `current`. The whole loop's correctness therefore rests on the unstated assumption `exit > candidate`, which `TryGetExclusionRegionExit` (764-794) does not enforce: for a Days/Dates match the exit is `WallClock.ToUtc(nextMidnight, exclusionZone, candidate).Utc`, and `WallClock.ToUtc` resolves an AMBIGUOUS wall time to the LARGEST offset, i.e. the EARLIEST of the two instants (WallClock.cs:97-101, 118-119). If a zone's fall-back moves the clock back ACROSS midnight, the first pass of the next local midnight is followed by instants that read as the excluded date again, so the recomputed exit is <= the candidate the loop currently stands on.
ledger.failure_scenario: Cron schedule `0 * * * *` with `InTimeZone(z)` and `Except(e => e.OnDays(DayOfWeek.Saturday))`, on a zone whose DST fall-back is at 00:30 local going back one hour to 23:30 of the previous date (so `IsAmbiguousTime(midnight)` is true and instants after that midnight map back to the excluded date). Candidate lands in the repeated window: `exit` = first pass of the next midnight <= candidate; `baseGrid.CronInterval.GetNextOccurrence(exit - 1 tick, zone)` (line 726-727) answers a slot AT OR BEFORE the candidate. Two outcomes, both wrong: (a) that earlier slot is still excluded → the loop re-derives the same exit and re-asks Cronos from the same instant, spinning until the 200,000-candidate budget throws `ExclusionSearchBudgetExceededException` on a perfectly healthy schedule (which then parks the series with backoff and eventually poisons it); (b) that earlier slot is NOT excluded → `GetNextOccurrence` returns an instant <= the `current` it was asked to advance past, so the caller schedules an occurrence in the past — it fires immediately and spends a run (exactly the failure gotcha 7 exists to prevent). Independently of the DST trigger, the absence of the guard means any future exit-computation bug degrades into an infinite-ish loop or a backwards answer rather than a clean stop.
ledger.evidence: RecurringTask.cs:686-714 (loop with no `candidate <= current` check); RecurringTask.cs:724-730 (cron branch computes from `exit` alone, never compared to `candidate`); RecurringTask.cs:776-780 (exit from `WallClock.ToUtc(nextMidnight, exclusionZone, candidate)`); WallClock.cs:97-101 and 118-119 (ambiguous wall time resolves to the LARGEST offset = the EARLIEST instant); contrast the guards at RecurringTask.cs:973 and 1017.
ledger.fix_sketch: Add the same defensive bail the sibling walks carry: after `candidate = AdvanceBasePastExcludedRegion(...)`, `if (candidate is { } next && next <= current) return null;` (or, better, clamp in `AdvanceBasePastExcludedRegion` by falling back to `GetNextBaseOccurrence(baseGrid, candidate, ...)` whenever the region-jump answer is not strictly greater than `candidate`).

votes.reasoning:
NOT REFUTED (mechanism confirmed), but severity/reachability materially overstated.

Confirmed by construction:
- The loop at RecurringTask.cs:693-711 has no forward-progress bail; the cron branch at 724-730 computes the next slot from `exit.AddTicks(-1)` as an absolute instant, never compared to `candidate`/`current`.
- `exit <= candidate` is achievable with a REAL zone. Condition: a local midnight M strictly inside a fall-back ambiguity window (W_start < M < W_end), so the candidate can be in the second pass with wall date D while WallClock.ToUtc resolves M to its FIRST pass (largest offset, WallClock.cs:97-101/118-119). Verified live against TimeZoneInfo 'America/St_Johns' (fall-back at 00:01 -> 23:01): candidate = wall 2005-10-29 23:15 second pass = 2005-10-30 02:45Z (wall date Saturday, excluded); exit = ToUtc(2005-10-30 00:00) = 2005-10-30 02:30Z, i.e. 15 min BEFORE the candidate. Cronos asked from 02:29:59.9999999Z then answers 02:30Z (wall 00:00 Sunday, not excluded) => GetNextOccurrence(current=02:40Z) returns 02:30Z, a value < current. With `30 * * * *` the same exit is re-derived from the same candidate each pass -> spins to the 200k budget and throws ExclusionSearchBudgetExceededException. Both outcomes (a) and (b) reproduce.
- No downstream clamp: NextOccurrenceStrictlyAfter delegates straight to GetNextOccurrence(after) for cron (line 932); SelectNextRun returns `next` unchecked when CurrentRun > 0 (line 511). So a past value reaches the scheduler.

Where the finding is wrong / overstated:
- The scenario's zone is fictional. I scanned all 141 system zones x all adjustment rules for an end-transition time-of-day strictly inside the daylight delta: the only hits are Newfoundland, all with DateEnd <= 2010-12-31. No zone falls back at 00:30; no zone has a midnight-straddling ambiguity window in current or future rules. Boundary cases (Chile/Brazil 24:00 -> 23:00, Cuba/Palestine 01:00 -> 00:00) are provably safe because midnight is then the window's exclusive upper bound or its inclusive start, and candidate and exit share the same offset. DST gaps are also safe: a Shifted midnight maps to the transition instant, which is always > any instant whose wall reads the previous date. So a schedule evaluating present/future instants cannot hit this; it needs a deliberate BackfillFrom / hand-set cursor into a pre-2011 Newfoundland fall-back window (<=59 minutes, twice-never since 2010), with cron + Days/Dates exclusions in that zone.
- "unlike every other walk" applies only to the cron branch. The uniform branch is immune: TryJumpUniformGrid takes first = GetNextOccurrence(anchor) and returns it when first > after (1292-1296), so a bogus `after` degrades into a one-step anchored advance. The calendar/provider branch (line 732) advances from `candidate` and never reads `exit`. Range exclusions cannot produce a bad exit (ToUtc > candidate is the match condition, 786-790).

Verdict: genuine missing-guard defect with a real, if historical-only, repro; correct fix is a `next <= candidate` fallback to the anchored advance (or a `candidate <= current` bail in the loop). Realistic rating P3 hardening, not P2 "healthy schedule poisoned". Confidence medium: the repro arithmetic is verified against live tz data, but the zone scan used Windows registry rules (141 zones) rather than full tzdata, so I cannot fully exclude an exotic historical zone on Linux widening the window.

The finding's structural observation is true (the cron branch has no `next <= candidate` bail), but the claimed failure is unreachable and two of the three regimes already carry the guard.

(1) Existing guards inside the loop's own advance: the non-uniform/non-cron branch (RecurringTask.cs:732) ignores `exit` and advances strictly from `candidate` via GetNextBaseOccurrence — forward by construction. The uniform branch (:721-722 -> TryJumpUniformGrid :1286-1296) begins with `first = GetNextOccurrence(anchor=candidate); if (first.Value > after) return first;` — when `exit <= candidate`, `after = exit-1 < candidate < first`, so it returns the next real slot AFTER the candidate. That is precisely the no-progress bail, expressed as a fast path; a backwards exit cannot yield a backwards or repeated answer there.

(2) The ranges half of TryGetExclusionRegionExit enforces the assumption explicitly: :786 skips any range with `candidate >= range.ToUtc`, and :789-790 only ever raises the exit. So `exit > candidate` is a checked contract for ranges, and range exits can never lower a days/dates exit.

(3) The Days/Dates midnight exit is > candidate for every zone shape that exists. The wall->instant map is monotone within a pass, and the exit is midnight of localDate+1 while the candidate's wall time is on localDate. The only non-monotone case is the finding's own premise: a fall-back whose repeated window straddles local midnight (pre-transition local time strictly between 00:00 and the shift, e.g. 00:30 -> 23:30). I scanned every system time zone for every day 2020-2100 for exactly that condition (IsAmbiguousTime(midnight) AND IsAmbiguousTime(midnight - 1 tick)): 0 hits. The scan is proven functional — it finds the near misses: Cuba/Azores/Jordan/West Bank (01:00 -> 00:00, ambiguous window [00:00, 01:00)) and Chile/Iran/Paraguay/Egypt/Syria (00:00 -> 23:00, window [23:00 D-1, 00:00 D), endpoint exclusive). Both shapes keep exit > candidate: in the first, every instant whose local date is D-1 precedes the first pass of midnight D; in the second, 00:00 D is not ambiguous and takes the post-transition offset, landing after the second pass of 23:xx D-1. A DST GAP at midnight (present in several of those zones) pushes the exit LATER via FirstValidLocalTime — the safe direction.

(4) The "spins until the 200,000 budget throws" outcome is misdescribed: `discarded` increments every iteration and :707-708 throws ExclusionSearchBudgetExceededException, a bounded, typed, designed path (spec section 5.4: ingress refusal / recovery poison / advance re-park). There is no infinite loop.

What survives is a P3-grade consistency/defense-in-depth nit about the cron branch (:724-730) being the one regime whose forward progress rests on an unstated `exit > candidate`, unlike the explicit bails at :973 and :1017. Not the P2 defect described. Caveat: the zone scan used the Windows registry tz data on this host; I could not scan Linux/ICU IANA data directly, though the near-miss shapes it found match IANA's real transitions.

ledger.title: SkipOldest bisection and the Halt threshold on a filtered grid are named in §8 but untested
ledger.area: tests / catch-up on a filtered grid (§8)
ledger.invariant: Spec §8 "Counting": "`SkipOldest` bisection on a filtered grid; `Halt` threshold unaffected by excluded slots" — both are decisions taken from counts over the grid, and §2.3 promises the bisection and the Halt breaker "operate on the filtered grid".
ledger.causal_chain: The SkipOldest search (`FindNthSlotFromEndAsync` / the memoized bisection at DueSlotEnumerator.cs:720-770) and the Halt threshold count (`CountDueAsync` → `CountMissedAsync`, line 507) both reach the grid through `evaluator.NextAfterAsync` / `CountMissedAsync`, so they are filtered by construction today. But the bisection carries its own monotonicity assumption (it interpolates a slot index onto a tick range), and an exclusion makes the grid non-uniform in a way `IsUniformGrid()` now reports (`false`) while the bisection's probe arithmetic still assumes a workable density. No test in the 15 exclusion-touching test files sets `OverflowPolicy = CatchUpOverflowPolicy.SkipOldest` together with `Exclusions`, and the one Halt-configured test (`Should_replay_only_weekday_slots_when_catch_up_crosses_a_weekend`) never reaches the threshold.
ledger.failure_scenario: A catch-up schedule with `ExceptWeekends` and `SkipOldest` recovers from a multi-week outage. If the bisection's probe lands inside an excluded region and the memoized count for that probe is off by the region's worth of slots, the plan drops or replays a slot — a silent data-correctness failure in exactly the path §2.1 promises ("the `SkipOldest` bisection ... operate on the filtered grid"). Nothing in the suite would notice.
ledger.evidence: src/EverTask/Scheduler/Occurrences/DueSlotEnumerator.cs:720-770 (bisection) and :495-510 (Halt/diagnostic counts); grep over `test/` for files containing `Exclusions|ExceptWeekends|Except(` yields 15 files, none of which contain `SkipOldest`; the only `Halt` configuration beside exclusions is test/EverTask.Tests/IntegrationTests/DurableOccurrencesIntegrationTests.cs:186 (`OverflowPolicy = CatchUpOverflowPolicy.Halt`) where the backlog is two slots and the cap is 10.
ledger.fix_sketch: Add a `DueSlotEnumeratorTests` case with `CatchUpOverflowPolicy.SkipOldest`, a `MaxOccurrences` smaller than the backlog and `Exclusions.Days = [Saturday, Sunday]`, asserting the granted slots equal a brute-force filtered reference (the pattern `RecurringExclusionMathTests.Should_count_only_filtered_occurrences_and_honour_caps` already uses); and one Halt case where the excluded slots would push the count over the threshold if they were counted.

It needs only monotonicity of f(probe) = |filtered slots in (probe, now]|, which holds for any instant set; deleting slots cannot break it. `MaxBisectionSteps = 64` covers the full DateTimeOffset tick range (log2 ≈ 62), so termination is grid-independent. The probe is never an anchor — `NextAfterAsync(definition, firstSlot, probe)` anchors on firstSlot, a real occurrence, so a probe landing inside an excluded region resolves to the first non-excluded slot after it, exactly the full-enumeration answer.

(2) The memoized-chain hazard is unreachable with exclusions. The chain is provider-only (DueSlotEnumerator.cs:713, `definition.Provider is null ? null : …`), and RecurringTask.ValidateProvider throws InvalidOperationException when Exclusions != null beside a Provider (spec line 377 confirms this is intended). An exclusion-bearing definition can never take the memoized path, so "the memoized count is off by the region's worth of slots" is impossible.

1) The bisection does no density/interpolation arithmetic. `FindNthSlotFromEndAsync` (src/EverTask/Scheduler/Occurrences/DueSlotEnumerator.cs:704-772) is a plain midpoint binary search over the tick axis — `var mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;` (line 717) — not "a slot index interpolated onto a tick range" as the finding claims. Inside `DecideRecurringRunAsync` (Dispatcher.cs:1016-1075) S is normalized (it is a legal grid slot, so it comes back unchanged), it is not `> nowUtc`, and the grace-window branch `isRecovery && IsSlipedOccurrenceStillCurrentAsync(recurring, S, nowUtc, ...)` answers TRUE whenever S's natural successor is still in the future — the normal state seconds after a run on any cadence coarser than the retry backoff. The dispatcher therefore returns `RecurringRunDecision(S, false)`, logs `RecoveryExecutingSlippedOccurrence`, and parks the schedule at S, which is in the past, so the scheduler fires it immediately and the handler runs again. The same hole reopens on restart: the row on disk carries no marker distinguishing "this cursor's run already happened" from "this cursor is pending" (`ScheduleRunAlreadyRecorded` is memory-only, TaskHandlerExecutor.cs:97-101), so startup recovery re-dispatches S through the identical grace window.

The row is parked to retry in 30 s. At 08:00:30 the retry runs; by now the search succeeds (a tzdata update, or the operator repaired the definition). `RetryScheduleDecisionAsync` re-dispatches the row with `executionTime = 2026-01-05T08:00Z`; the successor is 2026-01-06T08:00Z > now, so the grace window says "still current" and the schedule is parked at 08:00Z — already past — and fires at once. rawCandidates.title: TryGetExclusionRegionExit dereferences the exclusion arrays without the null tolerance its three siblings implement
rawCandidates.invariant: A hand-built or hand-edited definition fails as typed, validated metadata (ArgumentException → poison path), never with a NullReferenceException out of the occurrence math. The exclusions feature adopts this rule explicitly everywhere else: `ValidateExclusions` repairs nulls (RecurringTask.cs:233-235), `HasCalendarExclusions()` is written `(exclusions.Days?.Length ?? 0) > 0` (RecurringTask.cs:400-402) because spec §4.2 requires it to run BEFORE `Validate()`, and `AppendExclusions` uses `exclusions.Days ?? []` (RecurringTask.cs:1443-1445).
rawCandidates.causal_chain: `ScheduleExclusions.Days/Dates/Ranges` are plain `{ get; set; }` array properties with collection initializers and no converter (ScheduleExclusions.cs:13-20), so System.Text.Json writes a literal JSON `null` straight through the setter — which is exactly why `ValidateExclusions` opens with `exclusions.Days ??= []`. `TryGetExclusionRegionExit` is the per-candidate predicate on the evaluation path and reads `exclusions.Days.Length`, `exclusions.Dates.Length`, `exclusions.Days.Contains(...)`, `exclusions.Dates.Contains(...)` and `foreach (var range in exclusions.Ranges)` unguarded (RecurringTask.cs:769-791). `CalculateNextRun` / `CalculateNextValidRun` are PUBLIC surface (RecurringTask.cs:410-419, RecurringTaskExtensions.cs:42-49) and do not call `Validate()` themselves — only the library's own ingress and recovery paths do — so any consumer reaching the grid without validating gets an NRE from inside the scheduler instead of the documented ArgumentException.
